extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American government, public finance, and state-level public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook guidance on state taxation systems and legal/regulatory standards for controlling corporations, railroads, and other economic activity at the state level. Covers principles, constitutional constraints, typical tax types, administrative safeguards, and examples of state practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: General property tax — assessability limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When property consisted of tangible things ... it was easy for the assessor to secure a fairly complete and accurate list of the property of each resident within his district. However, when joint stock concerns and corporations came into existence, and persons could invest their wealth in bonds or stocks ... the assessors could no longer keep track of the property within their local units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why the general property tax became difficult to administer as economies commercialized and wealth became more intangible; motivates the move toward other sources of revenue (inheritance, corporation, excise, and special taxes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance tax — adoption, structure, and trends
rubrics_metrics.description: The inheritance tax ... has found favor in America only within recent years — practically since 1890, but it has now been adopted in some form by more than three-fourths of the states. The progressive rule increasing the rate with the amount of the inheritance is more frequently applied; the exemptions allowed to direct heirs are being lowered; and there is a tendency to apply it equally to real and personal property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete 1907 examples (highest rate 15% on collateral heirs in some states; highest exemptions amounts) and notes trends toward higher rates, progressive schedules, lower exemptions for direct heirs, and extension to personal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments for and against the inheritance tax
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument in favor: it is easy to collect, falls upon those ablest to bear it, and permits the state to secure revenue from intangible personal property; opponent argument: injurious to business because it withdraws capital from private enterprises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides normative considerations policy-makers weigh: ease and equity of collection vs. potential negative effects on investment and business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income tax — administrative safeguards to prevent evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Income tax has been employed ... but it has not proved popular nor effective on account of evasions. An attempt in Oklahoma to overcome administration difficulties requires all persons to certify under oath the excess of their incomes over $3,500; authorizes the assessor to send names of suspected persons to the state auditor; and empowers the auditor to resort to drastic measures to ascertain the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes concrete enforcement tools: sworn certifications, assessor reporting, auditor investigation and enforcement powers as administrative design elements to improve compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate taxation — multiple bases and interstate limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states tax all corporations on the actual value of their capital stock; others tax quasi‑public corporations according to their gross receipts or their earnings. In taxing them, the legislature is constantly harassed by perplexing problems ... and must also be careful not to come into conflict with the interstate commerce clause of the federal Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains alternative tax bases (capital stock, gross receipts, earnings), practical difficulties in apportioning value for multi‑state operations, reliance on corporate statements, and constitutional constraint (interstate commerce). Includes New York's specific formation tax and annual capital stock tax based on earning power as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation of liquor traffic — revenue and revenue-sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: All of the states which permit the sale of intoxicating liquors derive a revenue ... In New York, this tax on the liquor traffic amounts in some years to more than a fourth of the entire revenue of the commonwealth, but one-half of the amount collected by the state central government is returned to the communities from which it is derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates how excise taxes (liquor) can be major revenue sources and may be partially redistributed back to local jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and professional license taxes — regulatory and fiscal function
rubrics_metrics.description: A large proportion of the states ... employ business and professional taxes for state or local purposes. Nearly all commonwealths levy license taxes on dealers in liquor, peddlers, travelling vendors, and various kinds of amusements, primarily for regulation or suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows these taxes serve both regulatory/suppressive aims and revenue, with examples of jurisdictions levying many classes (Wilmington: 124 classes; Atlanta license ordinance: 466 items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of state and local taxation and the rise of special taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Result has been a revolution in the tax system of many states, New York having gone so far as to abandon altogether the general property tax for state purposes in favor of inheritance, corporation, excise, and other special taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the policy shift from a general property tax toward specialized taxes to capture revenue escaping local assessors and to allocate state vs local fiscal responsibilities; supported by New York revenue tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical state expenditure categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbursements of state governments are generally distributed ... among: (1) maintenance of the government in its executive, legislative, and judicial branches; (2) the state militia; (3) health and sanitation; (4) highways; (5) insane asylums; (6) charities; (7) penal institutions; (8) education; (9) interest on public state debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a canonical budget classification and an illustrative New York fiscal year itemized list with amounts to show priorities and scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of corporate chartering — general laws vs special acts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the beginning ... it was the practice of the state legislature to create each corporation by a separate law, but ... the legislature is now forbidden to create corporations by special act, and is authorized to pass only general laws providing equal terms for all corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States aim to obstruct granting special favors; examples: New York permits special acts only for municipal or where objects cannot be attained under general law; Delaware requires two‑thirds legislative approval for corporate laws in some contexts; Virginia issues charters through a commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendability of corporate charters and prohibition of irrevocable grants
rubrics_metrics.description: State constitutions now make provision for the future amendment, repeal, or alteration of general and special laws under which corporations may be created. Some states expressly forbid the irrevocable grant of any franchise, privilege, or immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional provisions allow regulation of corporations after creation, subject to limits protecting vested rights; quoted Alabama: no irrevocable or exclusive grants; but many constitutions also limit repeal/amendment so as not to impair vested rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stockholder protections and corporate internal governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal management of corporations is controlled ... several states have declared that each stockholder shall have one vote for each share. Nebraska requires laws providing the right to vote in person or by proxy, or to cumulate shares, and prohibits other methods of election of directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies governance safeguards: one‑vote‑per‑share principle, cumulative voting options, rights to vote by proxy, and statutory liabilities of directors to creditors and stockholders for embezzlement or misappropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention of stock‑watering and issuance controls
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent stock‑watering it is frequently provided by law that corporations shall not issue stock except for money, labor done, or property actually received to the amount of its par value; that stock and bonded indebtedness shall not be increased except in accordance with the general law and the consent of the persons holding the larger amount in value of the stock; and that fictitious issues of stock and indebtedness shall be deemed void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where public service commissions exist, corporations wishing to issue stock/bonds must file sworn, accurate statements showing exact purposes and obtain proper authorization — a procedural safeguard against dilution and fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of consolidations, combinations, and trusts
rubrics_metrics.description: The consolidation or combination of competing corporations is either forbidden altogether, or permitted under strict regulation. Example: Oklahoma — no public service corporation can consolidate or lease/purchase the works or franchises of any corporation owning a competing or parallel line except by legislative enactment upon recommendation of the state corporation commission; Montana expressly declares no corporation shall directly combine or form a trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes statutory/constitutional limits on mergers and inter‑ownership to prevent anti‑competitive concentration; some states allow consolidation only with legislative/commission approval and permit limited exceptions (e.g., pledging stock to secure bona fide indebtedness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroad/common carrier status and legislative control of rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Many states declare railways to be public highways and 'free to all persons for the transportation of their persons or property thereon under the regulations prescribed by law.' More recent state constitutions expressly authorize the legislature to fix passenger and freight rates and control railways generally so as to prevent unjust discriminations and maintain certain standards of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames railroads as regulated public utilities: legislative rate‑setting power, duty to prevent unjust discrimination and extortion, and authorization to enforce via penalties including forfeiture of property and franchise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat passenger fare laws and classification by earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: A wave of railroad rate regulation fixed flat rates of from two to three cents a mile in several states. In 1907 Illinois, Indiana, Minnesota, Nebraska, and Pennsylvania passed statutes fixing maximum passenger rate at two cents a mile. Some states classified roads according to their earnings per mile and fixed rates accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the historical policy instrument (flat maximum fares) and the follow‑on adaptation (classification by earnings) as responses to political pressure for fare reduction; notes legal and political pushback (vetoes, injunctions, compromises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of discriminatory practices and publicity requirements for carriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Railroads are commonly forbidden to discriminate in their charges or facilities between places or persons ... to issue free passes to state officials and members of the legislature; to grant rebates and bonuses; and to deny individuals, associations, and corporations similarly situated equal rights. Most states require publicity systems whereby each railway company must maintain a public office and publish statistics relative to its business, profits, dividends, transfer of stock, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets both substantive prohibitions (no discrimination, rebates, illicit passes) and transparency obligations (public offices, periodic publication of financial/business statistics) as tools to ensure fair treatment and enable oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical valuation and extensive financial accounting for rate regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some constitutions and laws have ordered the physical valuation of railroad property. Commissions must ascertain amounts expended in construction and equipment per mile; amounts to reconstruct; outstanding bonds and indebtedness (when issued, rate, purposes, to whom issued, price received, how proceeds used); floating indebtedness; credits; property on hand; judicial sales; salaries and wages; and keep such records as public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the detailed factual base regulators must develop to determine reasonable rates: valuation of property, apportionment between intra‑state and interstate operations, exhaustive accounting of debt and expenditures, and labor costs — a procedural/technical rubric for informed rate‑making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory adaptability — limits of positive enactment and role of administrative commissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers find it impossible to control, by positive enactment, all of the multifarious operations of railway and other public service corporations, and they have discovered also that the same rule cannot be applied equally to all companies in all parts of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifies use of commissions, adjudicative processes, case‑by‑case regulation and discretionary administrative machinery to handle complexity and local variation rather than rigid blanket statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and statutory prohibitions on monopolies, primogeniture, and perpetuities
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations and trusts to enhance prices and restrain trade ... are expressly prohibited and declared to be unlawful and against public policy. Constitutions have abolished primogeniture; Oklahoma declares 'Perpetuities and monopolies ... shall never be allowed,' and forbids law of primogeniture or entailments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies constitutional expressions of public policy favoring competition and preventing concentration of land/wealth: bans on trusts/monopolies, limits on land grants to individuals (e.g., public lands sold only to actual settlers, acreage limits), and abolition of primogeniture.
